1.  When Gotcha explains what inspired “Turning a Blind Eye”, what does
     she say is behind the feeling of defeat?
   ■  The pressure of competing with other contemporary Australian musicians.
   ■  Her inability to adapt to present-day Australian lifestyle.
   ■  Her awareness of how everyday habits lead to overconsumption.
   ■ A disappointment about how little artists care about technology.
2.   Gotcha finds it difficult to change her environmental habits because
   ■   it’s hard to know what really helps.
   ■  there is too much information, she feels overwhelmed.
   ■  she thinks no one else is making an effort.
   ■   it’s difficult to change long-established habits.

   ■  She is idealistic most of the time, so her songs are optimistic despite

   ■  The contrast between her environmentally friendly lifestyle and that
         of other musicians.
   ■ How travelling constantly increases her environmental impact.
   ■ How certain hotels contribute to the overall carbon footprint.
   ■ How each culture approaches environmental problems differently.
5.  How does Gotcha feel about her growing success?
   ■  She thinks success always brings joy to anyone.
   ■  She fears larger projects will feel less meaningful to her.

   ■  She feels that social media makes followers focus on what she says

SÈRIE 1


I. Listening comprehension (3 points)

“AN INTERVIEW WITH GOTCHA, THE MUSICAL FORCE!”

In this podcast you are going to hear some new words. Read and listen to them. Make
sure you know what they mean.

to quote: citar textualment / citar textualmente

prone: propens/propenso

bouts: período/período

harp: arpa/arpa

Ready? Now read the questions on the following page. Read them carefully before
listening to the podcast. [Now listen to the interview.]

Interviewer (I): You are Gotcha, the musical force!

Gotcha (G): Haha, from now on I’m going to introduce myself as Gotcha, the musical
force. My real name is Margot Chapman, but I guess I’ve got used to being called
Gotcha more often now.

I: Right, I got you. That song we’ve just listened to, ‘Turning a Blind Eye’, is the first
Australian single from your latest record, Making Miracles. It's a song that you say
describes your feelings of being completely defeated, I'm quoting you, “by the realities
of living in contemporary Australia.” What's been difficult about life there?

G: Oh, it's not specifically about living in contemporary Australia, although I’m
American. It comes from a place of defeat, I guess, in the sense of being someone who
is concerned, maybe a bit more aware than some people, in terms of how things I do in
my regular life, in terms of use of materials, driving cars, using so much disposable
technology to make music, how that is so implicitly involved in so much... use, maybe
overuse of resources?

I: Your carbon footprint.

G: Yeah. And I feel very conflicted about the reliability of the information available.
When I try to research it and make changes, it’s incredibly hard to find a clear basis for
making informed judgments or decisions. It’s hard to feel like anything I do makes a
difference, even in my own life. Whether or not it sets an example for my fans or helps
spread a more environmental message, sometimes it just feels like I’m making
changes simply to avoid feeling completely defeated.
                                                                      Pàgina 2 de 7
                                                                       Anglès
Proves d’accés a la Universitat 2026, convocatòria ordinària. Criteri específic d'avaluació

I: But the feeling of being “completely defeated” when you were writing this song
suggests that you're quite pessimistic about our future. Are you?

G: I have moments like that, yeah. I sometimes change my mind a lot when I compose.
You know, I think I'm an idealist a lot of the time, but often prone to bouts of very
depressive cycles of thought and pessimism about the potential for really fundamental
change in the way humans live on earth, at least. It's those moments when I feel like
that really prompted the lyrics to ‘Turning a Blind Eye’.

I: And what about the fact that now that you’re touring, you’re inevitably traveling more
and experiencing not just different countries, but different cultures and different ways
people are trying to deal with issues like the environment and ecological change? Does
that make you feel more defeated, or do you find things on those travels that inspire
you?

G: You know, touring for a music career does involve seeing a lot of airports, hotel
rooms, cars, buses, et cetera, though some artists do it more than I do. Even so, I'm
probably more in touch with the reality of having an ever-increasing carbon footprint, at
least in terms of what I'm doing in my music career. And it is indeed something I think
about.

I: So you wrote the song ‘Turning a Blind Eye’ feeling completely defeated. It's getting
worse now because the song's popular and your carbon footprint is harming
everybody.

G: Haha. I do think about that. It's funny, more and more people tell me, I must be so
overjoyed and amazed by the success and how big everything's getting. But I guess
part of what makes me worry and that might lead to writing a song like this, is the
sense that the bigger things get, the less likely they are to stay sustainable or be
personal. I don't know...

I: And not just environmentally, but materially, emotionally.

G: Emotionally, yeah, trying to communicate with increasing numbers of people. I feel a
bit freaked out about it. I think I have a different approach. It’s difficult for me to even
write anything on my Twitter account; even though it's not like I have a huge number of
people following me there, only around 40, 50,000. I still think about it. I know plenty of
people have millions of followers on these social media. But even so, realizing that my
audience is broader now, and that lots of different kinds of people are discovering my
music, changes how aware I am of who I’m speaking to on these platforms.

I: Let me talk a bit about the record, Making Miracles. You're getting a lot of attention
for this record, and that's got to be rewarding given the amount of work that you put
into it. You play most of the instruments on it, but even more remarkable is the method
of taking acoustic instruments, recording them note by note, and then turning them into
virtual instruments. What exactly does that mean you're doing in terms of creating
these sounds?
                                                                      Pàgina 3 de 7
                                                                       Anglès
Proves d’accés a la Universitat 2026, convocatòria ordinària. Criteri específic d'avaluació

G: Yes, it’s the case of a harp that I found at an antique shop. A harp is not particularly
a new-sounding instrument. It's one you've probably heard. The way it sounds on a
record is usually quite angelic, because that's the way you can play it, but to record it
note by note and then have control over those notes just means that you make the
instrument sound incredible. It almost turns into a completely new instrument.

I: That's remarkably creative and innovative, but where does that come from? I mean,
do you have an allergy to just playing an acoustic guitar and singing a song?

G: Well, I'm really excited by alternative ways of making music. They open up windows
to sound worlds I haven't explored before, and those are the kinds of records I want to
make. I'm not against using traditional instruments: there's plenty of piano and regular
drum kits on the album, but I have a pretty intense interest in things like, what if you
could use... a plastic ball and use that as a drum instead of just getting a drum out and
putting a mic on it. It's just more interesting. It just means there's more of a story. I
guess it creates a far greater range of textures, though it also takes time.

I: This is so interesting, Gotcha, but I’m afraid we have run out of time. It’s been a
pleasure to have you here with us today.

G: Nice to chat, too.

reading.examen:
Reading · PAU 2026 · Juny · Sèrie 1

    Part 2: Reading comprehension

                WHAT’S AFTER UMAMI? SCIENTISTS ARE HUNTING
                        FOR THE SIXTH BASIC TASTE
         In 1908, Japanese chemist Kikunae Ikeda was studying the active substances in seaweed, when
        he made a discovery that would change food science forever. Ikeda realized that a compound
          called glutamic acid was what gave seaweed its distinctive taste—nothing like the existing basic
           tastes of sweet, salty, sour, and bitter. He named that taste umami.
     5      Yet even though people have been eating seaweed, mushrooms, miso, cheese, and
         fermented foods for ages, it took nearly a century of scientific debate for umami to be recognized
        worldwide as the fifth basic taste. It wasn’t until the 1990s that it gained universal recognition,
        and only after extensive scientific studies confirmed that it was unlike any other existing taste.
                 Is it time to add a sixth taste to the list? Some scientists argue that the answer is yes, though
    10  there is still debate about what it should be. Scientists have not been intentionally searching
          for a sixth taste. Rather, “there’s a fundamental science-based search for different ways we can
         experience the world in terms of taste and how it’s detected,” explains neuroscientist Emily Liman.
            Advances in understanding the science of taste would allow food scientists to create more
          delicious foods—and could also help doctors diagnose and treat related disorders that involve a
    15   loss of your sense of taste. But getting the scientific community to agree on a sixth sense is not
          easy. To qualify as a basic taste, any competitor must be proven to be as distinct as the sweetness
          of berries or the bitterness of kale.
                 First, it’s important to note that “there’s a difference between taste and flavor,” says Marisa
        Moore, a dietitian in culinary nutrition from Atlanta. “Taste begins on the tongue when food
    20  molecules we eat mix with saliva and activate our taste buds, which then send signals to the
         brain and cause the perception of distinct tastes.” Contrary to popular belief, the tongue does
         not have specific areas that detect each type of taste. Instead, basic tastes can be picked up by
           taste buds on various parts of the tongue, though different cells may have varying levels of
           sensitivity to sweet, sour, salty, bitter, and umami.
    25      While taste begins in the mouth, flavor is what registers in the brain when it combines
         the entire experience of taste, texture, temperature, and aroma. “Taste and other senses do
          interact in the brain to put together flavor,” says Richard Mattes, professor of nutrition science
           at Purdue University, “but that’s different from taste.”
             Various criteria have been proposed over the years to define a new taste. For starters, a taste
    30  needs to have a “chemical signature”—a set of chemical components that are distinct from that
          of other substances. Then, Mattes says, “you need to have a receptor anywhere on the tongue,
          palate, or throat where the chemical component can interact with a cell in a taste bud.” That cell
          in the taste bud must then have a mechanism “to change the component’s chemical signal to an
           electrical signal that is then transmitted through nerves to the brain,” Mattes adds. The electrical
    35  signal carried by taste nerves must activate regions in the brain that are associated with taste, and
              it needs to generate a unique taste perception in the brain that is independent from other tastes.
           Finally, there needs to be a response in the body that results from these effects. For example,
         Mattes says, “the perception of sweetness triggers the release of insulin throughout the body.”
             In short, a major challenge to getting the scientific community to accept a new taste has to
    40  do with the complexity of the research that needs to be conducted. “You have to go through a
           lot to prove a taste exists,” says Dawn Jackson Blatner, a dietitian nutritionist in Chicago. None
          of the candidates for a sixth basic taste have passed all experimental tests yet—but some of them
          are closer to doing so than others. Despite all these complications, scientists continue to study
        taste—and debate what the next big one might be—because taste is important, as it is about
    45  what we crave, how we cook, and how satisfied we feel after eating.

                                                                         Text adapted from an article by
                                             Stacey Colino. National Geographic [online] (November 25, 2025)
